rentBurden.flag: Housing takes {pct}% of your income. Over 35% is a warning sign.

rentBurden.evidenceRenter: Renegotiating at renewal or sharing with a roommate usually cuts

tips.ownerRate: Ask 2–3 banks for a cheaper mortgage rate.
tips.ownerTax: Appeal your property tax if similar homes are valued lower.
tips.ownerInsurance: Drop mortgage insurance once you own 20% of the home.
tips.renterLease: Ask your landlord for a discount if you sign a longer lease.
tips.renterRoommate: Think about a roommate or a smaller place at renewal.
tips.renterCompare: Look at other listings 2 months before renewal to compare.

insuranceRequote.label: Insurance
insuranceRequote.title: Get new insurance quotes every year
insuranceRequote.why: Shown because your insurance ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
insuranceRequote.evidence: Shopping around every year usually cuts

tips.quotes: Get 3 quotes before your policy renews.
tips.bundle: Put home and car with one insurer for a discount.
tips.excess: Choose a higher excess you could pay from savings.

utilitiesEfficiency.label: Electricity & gas
utilitiesEfficiency.title: Small energy-saving habits
utilitiesEfficiency.why: Shown because your electricity and gas ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
utilitiesEfficiency.evidence: Turning heating or cooling down at night, switching off standby devices and using LED bulbs usually cuts

tips.night: Turn heating or AC down a few degrees at night and when you’re out.
tips.standby: Switch TVs and chargers off at the wall.

smartThermostat.label: Electricity & gas
smartThermostat.title: Install a smart thermostat
smartThermostat.why: Shown because your electricity and gas ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
smartThermostat.evidence: A smart thermostat that turns things down for you usually trims a further

tips.rebate: Check if your power company gives money back for one.
tips.away: Turn on the setting that lowers it when everyone leaves.
tips.report: Look at its monthly report and fix the most wasteful days.

electricitySlab.label: Electricity
electricitySlab.title: Stay under the next price slab
electricitySlab.why: Shown because your electricity bill ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
electricitySlab.evidence: Each unit costs more once you pass a slab, so keeping usage just under the next one usually cuts

tips.units: Find “units used” on your bill. Prices per unit jump at each slab, so aim to stay just under the next one.
tips.ac: Run the AC at 26°C with a ceiling fan on, and use timer or eco mode at night.
tips.peak: Run the iron, washing machine and water pump outside peak hours.

utilitiesTuneup.label: Electricity & gas
utilitiesTuneup.title: Quick energy tune-up
utilitiesTuneup.why: Shown because your electricity and gas ({amount}) is close to typical. A few small fixes still help.
utilitiesTuneup.evidence: Quick fixes like washing clothes in cold water and a water-saving shower head usually cut

tips.cold: Wash clothes in cold water and only run full loads.
tips.heater: Turn the water heater down a little.

internetRenegotiate.label: Internet & phone
internetRenegotiate.title: Ask your provider for a better deal
internetRenegotiate.why: Shown because your internet and phone bill ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
internetRenegotiate.evidence: Calling your provider and asking for a better deal usually cuts

tips.localBundle: Switch your mobile to a monthly prepaid bundle instead of loading balance as you go.
tips.localWifi: Use Wi-Fi calling and WhatsApp at home instead of mobile minutes.
tips.localPackage: Ask your internet provider for a cheaper package if you use less than half your speed.
tips.newCustomer: Call and ask for the deal new customers get.
tips.speedTest: Do a speed test. If you use less than half, pick a cheaper plan.
tips.prepaid: Compare prepaid phone plans on the same network.

fuelCarpool.label: Fuel
fuelCarpool.title: Carpool and combine errands
fuelCarpool.why: Shown because your fuel bill ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
fuelCarpool.evidence: Sharing school runs and doing errands in one trip usually cuts

tips.schoolRuns: Share school runs with 2 or 3 nearby families.
tips.errands: Do all your errands in one trip each week.
tips.tyres: Check tyre pressure once a month.

fuelCarlight.label: Fuel
fuelCarlight.title: Use the car less in the city
fuelCarlight.why: Shown because your fuel bill ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
fuelCarlight.evidence: Walking, cycling or taking public transport for short trips usually cuts

tips.walk: Walk or cycle for trips under 2 km.
tips.bigShops: Use the car only for big weekly shops.
tips.pass: Compare your fuel and parking costs with a monthly transport pass.

fuelHybridCommute.label: Fuel
fuelHybridCommute.title: Commute fewer days a week
fuelHybridCommute.why: Shown because your fuel bill ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
fuelHybridCommute.evidence: Working from home one or two days a week usually cuts

tips.wfh: Ask your manager for 1–2 work-from-home days.
tips.share: Share rides with a colleague who lives nearby.
tips.smooth: Drive smoothly: gentle starts use less fuel.

transitPass.label: Fares & tolls
transitPass.title: Get a monthly pass or toll tag
transitPass.why: Shown because your fares and tolls ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
transitPass.evidence: A monthly pass or toll tag usually cuts

tips.compare: Add up last month’s fares and compare with a monthly pass.
tips.tollTag: Get a toll tag for cheaper tolls.
tips.employer: Ask your employer if they help pay for travel.

carRefinance.label: Car loan
carRefinance.title: Look for a cheaper car loan
carRefinance.why: Shown because your car loan payment ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
carRefinance.evidence: Moving the loan to a lender with a lower interest rate usually cuts

tips.banks: Ask 2–3 banks for their car loan rate.
tips.term: Keep the same number of months left so you don’t pay for longer.
tips.fee: Check there’s no fee for paying the old loan off early.

groceriesPlan.label: Groceries
groceriesPlan.title: Plan meals and buy store brands
groceriesPlan.why: Shown because your grocery bill ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
groceriesPlan.evidence: Planning meals and buying store brands usually cuts

tips.plan: Plan the week’s meals before you shop, and stick to the list.
tips.localBulk: Buy monthly staples (flour, rice, oil, lentils, sugar) once a month in bulk from a wholesale market.
tips.storeBrand: Buy the shop’s own brand for basics like rice, flour and oil.
tips.bigPacks: Buy big packs of things you always use.
tips.freeze: Cook extra and freeze portions for later.

diningSwap.label: Eating out
diningSwap.title: Cook at home more often
diningSwap.why: Shown because you spend more eating out ({dining}) than on groceries ({groceries}).
diningSwap.evidence: Cooking at home a few more nights a week usually cuts

tips.swap: Swap 2 takeaway nights a week for quick home meals.
tips.lunch: Take lunch to work on weekdays.
tips.special: Keep eating out for special occasions.

impulse24h.label: Impulse shopping
impulse24h.title: Wait 24 hours before you buy
impulse24h.why: Shown because your impulse shopping ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
impulse24h.evidence: People who wait 24 hours before buying usually cut

tips.wait: Wait a day before buying anything you don’t need.
tips.cards: Remove saved card details from shopping apps.
tips.notifications: Turn off shop notifications and sale emails.

schoolDiscounts.label: School fees & childcare
schoolDiscounts.title: Ask about school discounts
schoolDiscounts.why: Shown because your school and childcare costs ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
schoolDiscounts.evidence: Asking for sibling or pay-early discounts usually saves

tips.siblings: Ask the school about discounts for brothers and sisters.
tips.upfront: Ask if paying for the year up front costs less.

medicalGeneric.label: Doctor & medicine
medicalGeneric.title: Ask for generic medicines
medicalGeneric.why: Shown because your doctor and medicine costs ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
medicalGeneric.evidence: Choosing generic medicines with the same active ingredient usually cuts

tips.generic: Ask your doctor or pharmacist for the generic version. It has the same active ingredient and costs less.
tips.monthlyPack: Buy medicines you take every month in a monthly pack, not strip by strip.
tips.localCover: Check if your employer’s health cover or a hospital card pays for doctor visits.
tips.insurance: Check what your health insurance or employer plan already pays for.

subsCancelUnused.label: Unused subscriptions
subsCancelUnused.title: Cancel what you rarely use
subsCancelUnused.why: Shown because you said you rarely use: {names}.

tips.cancel: Cancel them today. You can usually sign up again later.
tips.trials: Look at your bank statement for free trials that became paid.
tips.reminder: Set a reminder 2 days before any new free trial ends.

subsRotate.label: Streaming
subsRotate.title: Keep one streaming service at a time
subsRotate.why: Shown because your streaming and games subscriptions ({amount}) is higher than what's typical for {group} ({threshold}).
subsRotate.evidence: Keeping one service at a time and choosing cheaper plans usually cuts

tips.one: Keep one streaming service, then switch next month.
tips.ads: Choose the plan with ads, or pay yearly if it’s cheaper.
tips.family: Share a family plan with people in your home.

subsToolsYearly.label: Work & AI tools
subsToolsYearly.title: Pay yearly and drop overlapping tools

subsToolsYearly.evidence: Switching to yearly billing and cancelling tools that do the same job usually cuts

tips.employer: Ask your employer to pay for tools you use for work.

debtAvalanche.title: Move the balance to a 0% card

text.profile: Pick the household most like yours. We compare your bills with similar homes, so the tips fit your life.
text.currency: Changes the money symbol and the “typical” amounts we compare your bills with.
text.period: Show every amount per month or per year. Your numbers stay the same; only the display changes.
text.income: The money that reaches your bank account each month after tax. Use your take-home pay, not your salary before tax.
text.rent: What you pay each month to rent your home, or your mortgage payment if you’re buying it.
text.homeIns: Insurance that pays out if your home or belongings are damaged or stolen. Leave empty if you don’t have it.
text.electricity: Your average monthly electricity bill. If it changes with the seasons, use a rough average.
text.waterGas: Your monthly water and gas bills added together.
text.internet: Home internet plus mobile phone bills, added together.
text.fuel: Petrol or diesel for all your vehicles in a month.
text.transit: Bus, train, ride-hailing fares and road tolls in a month.
text.carIns: Car insurance per month. If you pay once a year, divide the yearly cost by 12.
text.carLoan: Your monthly car loan or lease payment.
text.school: School fees, tuition, day care or babysitting per month.
text.groceries: Food and household items you buy at shops and markets.
text.dining: Restaurants, cafés, takeaways and food delivery.
text.misc: Shopping you didn’t plan: clothes, gadgets, gifts, online orders and treats.
text.medical: Doctor visits, tests and medicine in a typical month. If it changes a lot, use a rough average.
text.homeHelp: Wages for a maid, cook, driver, guard or babysitter who helps at home.
text.familySupport: Money you regularly send to parents or other family members.
text.giving: Donations to charity and religious giving, such as zakat, tithes or offerings at your mosque, church or temple, as a monthly amount.
text.other: Any regular monthly cost that doesn’t fit the boxes above, like pet food, a committee payment or tuition classes.
text.extraAmount: The total you expect for the whole year, after tax. We divide it by 12 and add it to your monthly income. For overtime that changes, use a rough yearly total.
text.yearlyCost: The total for the whole year. We divide it by 12 to show what to put aside each month.
text.emergencyFund: Money you’ve already put aside for surprises, like losing your job or a big repair. This is a total, not a monthly amount.
text.debtName: A name to recognise this card or loan, like “Bank card”.
text.debtType: Credit cards usually charge much more interest than loans.
text.debtBalance: How much you still owe on this card or loan today.
text.debtApr: The yearly interest rate (APR): the extra the lender charges each year for borrowing, as a percentage. You’ll find it on your statement. Lower is better.
text.debtPayment: How much you pay towards this card or loan each month.
text.subName: The service, like Netflix or a gym.
text.subCost: What it costs each month. If you pay yearly, divide by 12.
text.subKind: What kind of subscription this is. We guess it from the name; change it if we got it wrong. Work tools count as a must-pay bill, the rest as nice-to-haves.
text.subRarely: Tick this if you used it fewer than twice last month. We’ll suggest cancelling it.
text.housingFree: Some people own their home outright or live with family for free. If that’s you, we won’t count housing against you.
text.summary: A one-line overview of your money, based on the numbers you entered.
text.spendNow: All the monthly bills you entered, added up.
text.spendCould: Your bills after the changes you added to your plan.
text.saveMonth: The money freed up each month by the changes in your plan. Interest you avoid on debt isn’t counted here.
text.top3: The three biggest savings we found, with the easiest one at the top. A good place to start.
text.health: A score from 0 to 100 that checks five things: saving, housing, debt, emergency fund and nice-to-haves. Higher is better.
text.split: Compares your spending with a common guideline: about half on must-pay bills, a third on nice-to-haves and a fifth saved.
text.categories: Each bar shows how much of your income goes to that area. The thin line shows what’s typical for households like yours.
text.payday: A short checklist for the day your pay arrives: put money aside for yearly costs, save first, and keep a weekly limit for spending. Tick each step off every month.
text.allowance: Your eating out and shopping budget after the ideas in your plan, split into weeks. Spending a fixed amount each week is easier to stick to than a monthly total.
text.plan: Ideas to spend less, based on your bills. Add the ones you’ll really do to your plan; only those count.
text.cut: Move the slider to the share you really think you can cut. Not sure? Keep our suggestion.
text.addToPlan: Only changes you add count towards your savings, charts and goal dates.
text.interestAvoided: Interest is the extra money a lender charges you. Avoiding it doesn’t put cash in your pocket today, but your debt gets paid off sooner.
text.years: How long you keep saving. More years give your money more time to grow.
text.rate: How much your savings grow each year on average. Safe accounts grow slowly; investing can grow faster but goes up and down.
text.inflation: Prices rise over time, so the same money buys less in future. This shows future amounts in today’s money.
text.allocation: This is the money left each month after your bills and your plan. Choose how to share it between your emergency fund, your debt and your goals.
text.goals: Things you’re saving for. We work out when you’ll reach each one using the share of savings you give to goals.
text.emergency: Money kept aside for surprises like losing your job or a car repair. Aim for 3 to 6 months of essential bills.
text.debtFree: When your loans would be fully paid off: now, and if you put your debt share of savings towards them.
text.history: Save a snapshot each month to see whether your spending is going down over time.
text.customAmount: What it costs in a normal month. Choose “Must-pay bill” if you can’t skip it, or “Nice-to-have” if you could cut it.

guide.title: 5 Hidden Household Expense Leaks (And How to Plug Them Today)
guide.intro1_html: Most households don't have a spending problem so much as a leak problem. The big, visible costs, such as rent, a mortgage or a car payment, get scrutinized constantly. Meanwhile, dozens of small, recurring charges quietly drain hundreds every month without anyone noticing. Because these leaks are automatic, spread out and individually small, they slip past even careful budgeters.
guide.intro2: The good news? Leaks are usually the easiest money to recover. Unlike cutting back on things you love, plugging a leak typically means paying less for exactly the same lifestyle. Here are the five most common hidden household expense leaks, and the practical steps you can take today to stop each one.

leak1.body_html: Every television, game console, coffee maker and phone charger left plugged in draws a trickle of electricity around the clock. This "phantom load", also called vampire power, can account for 5–10% of a typical home's electricity bill. Add heating or air conditioning running in an empty house, and old bulbs still lurking in lamps, and your power bill carries a lot of dead weight.
leak1.fix1_html: Use switched power strips for the TV corner and home office so idle devices switch off completely.
leak1.fix2_html: Turn heating down or air conditioning up by 4–6°C (7–10°F) while you sleep or are away. A timer or smart thermostat can do this for you.
leak1.fix3_html: Swap remaining bulbs for LEDs, which use up to 75% less energy and last many times longer.
leak1.fix4: Wash laundry in cold water and set your water heater or geyser to about 50°C (120°F).

leak2.body_html: Streaming services, cloud storage, app memberships, meal kits, fitness apps and "free trials" that quietly converted to paid plans add up fast. Many families pay for several subscriptions they rarely use. Because each one feels cheap on its own, the total almost never gets examined.
leak2.fix1_html: Pull your last three months of bank and card statements and list every recurring charge. Mark the ones you used less than twice last month.
leak2.fix2_html: Rotate streaming services instead of stacking them: subscribe to one, watch what you want, cancel and move to the next.
leak2.fix3: Call your internet and phone providers and ask the retention team for current promotional pricing, or drop to a speed tier you'll never notice.
leak2.fix4: Set a calendar reminder two days before any free trial ends.

leak3.title_html: 3Grocery Waste and the Dining-Out Premium
leak3.body_html: Many households throw away a surprising share of the food they buy. Pre-cut produce, single-serve packaging and unplanned mid-week trips all carry a convenience premium. Then there's eating out: when a household spends more on restaurants, takeaways and delivery than on groceries, it's usually paying several times more per meal for food it could make at home.
leak3.fix1_html: Plan meals around what's already in your fridge before writing a shopping list.
leak3.fix2: Choose store brands for staples. They're often made in the same places as big brands and usually cost less.
leak3.fix3: Shop once a week with a list, and schedule one "leftovers night" to clear the fridge.
leak3.fix4: Replace two takeaway nights a week with quick home recipes, and cook work lunches ahead at the weekend.

leak4.body_html: Fuel is one of the most variable costs in a household budget, and habits drive it. Short, scattered trips burn far more fuel per kilometre because engines are least efficient when cold. Under-inflated tyres, solo commuting and full-price tolls all add up. Insurance is the quieter twin of this leak. Premiums tend to creep up at every renewal, and insurers rarely reward loyalty, so households that never shop around often pay more than a new customer would.
leak4.fix1_html: Batch errands into a single loop once or twice a week, and organize a carpool for school runs or commuting.
leak4.fix2: Keep tyres properly inflated, which helps fuel economy and safety.
leak4.fix3: Compare monthly transport passes and toll tags against what you pay per trip.
leak4.fix4_html: Get new home and car insurance quotes every year, ask about multi-policy discounts, and consider a higher excess (deductible) that your emergency fund can cover.

leak5.body_html: The daily coffee, the late-night online order, the "it was on sale" purchase: impulse spending is the hardest leak to see because it never arrives as one bill. One-click checkout and saved card details remove the brief pause that would normally stop an unplanned purchase. When those purchases sit on a credit card charging high interest (the APR), the leak grows: a balance of 3,000 in any currency at 24% a year costs about 60 a month in interest alone.
leak5.fix1_html: Adopt the 24-Hour Rule: wait a full day before any non-essential purchase. Most urges fade.
leak5.fix2: Remove saved card details from shopping sites and turn off retailer notifications.
leak5.fix3_html: Pay the highest-interest loan first: pay the minimum on everything, and put every extra amount towards the debt with the highest interest rate.
leak5.fix4: Where they're offered, a 0% balance transfer card can help: a one-off fee of around 3% is often recovered within a few months of avoided interest.

wealth.title: Turn Plugged Leaks Into Real Wealth
wealth.p1_html: Plugging leaks only matters if the money goes somewhere useful. The most powerful step is to automate the savings immediately. The same week you cut a bill, set up an automatic transfer for that exact amount into a savings account that pays interest, your emergency fund or a low-cost investment fund. If the money never lands in your everyday bank account, it can't leak back out.
wealth.p2_html: Small numbers become large ones over time. Putting 250 a month (in any currency) into an investment averaging 8% a year grows to roughly 46,000 in ten years and more than 147,000 in twenty. Growth is never guaranteed. Use the calculator above to try your own numbers, add only the ideas that fit your life, and switch on “Show in today’s money” to allow for rising prices.
wealth.p3: Start with one leak this week. Check your subscriptions tonight, look at your heating or cooling settings tomorrow, and plan next week's meals at the weekend. Each fix takes minutes, and the savings repeat every month.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.q1: Is my financial data safe in this calculator?
faq.a1: Yes. Every calculation runs inside your web browser and nothing you type is sent to a server. Your numbers are only remembered in your own browser's local storage, and the reset button deletes them.
faq.q2: How are the savings estimates worked out?
faq.a2: Each idea takes the bill it's about and applies a careful, typical saving, for example 12% for energy-saving habits or 15% for carpooling. Open "How did we get this?" on any idea to see the exact sum. If two ideas cut the same bill, the second only counts what's left, so savings are never counted twice.
faq.q3: What does the "Add to my plan" switch do?
faq.a3: Only ideas you add to your plan count towards what you could spend, the money you could save, the growth chart, your goal dates and your debt-free date. Switch an idea off if it doesn't fit your life and every figure updates instantly.
faq.a4: It's a simple guideline: spend about half of your take-home pay on must-pay bills such as housing, power, groceries and loan payments, about a third on nice-to-haves such as eating out and subscriptions, and save about a fifth.
faq.q5: How is the budget health score calculated?
faq.a5: The score from 0 to 100 adds up five parts: how much you save each month (30 points), housing cost (20), debt (15), emergency savings (20) and spending on nice-to-haves (15). Each part has a sentence explaining your result and what to aim for.
faq.q6: Which growth rate should I pick for my savings?
faq.a6: A safe savings account has recently paid around 4% a year. Long-term investing in a broad mix of shares has averaged around 8% a year over long periods, but it goes up and down. Growth is never guaranteed, so try a few options and switch on "Show in today's money" to allow for rising prices.
faq.q7: How big should my emergency fund be?
faq.a7: A common guideline is 3 to 6 months of must-pay bills. Aim for the higher end if your household has one income, pay that changes, or people who depend on you. The tool shows how long you have now and how long it takes to reach each level.
faq.q8: Can I use rupees and other currencies?
faq.a8: Yes. Choose your country at the top of the page and the calculator uses its currency, typical household amounts and local tips. You can switch between USD, GBP, EUR, INR, PKR, AED, SAR, CAD, AUD, BRL, MXN, IDR and NGN, and rupee amounts are shown in lakh and crore. For other countries, typical amounts are worked out as shares of your income.

netIncome.definition: The money you actually receive after tax and other deductions. Use this number as your income.

emergencyFund.definition: Savings kept aside only for surprises, like losing your job or a big repair. A common goal is 3 to 6 months of must-pay bills.

apr.definition: The yearly cost of borrowing, shown as a percentage. At 30% APR, owing 100,000 for a whole year adds about 30,000 in interest.

compound.definition: When your savings earn money, and then that money earns money too. Over many years, savings grow faster and faster.

inflation.definition: Prices slowly rise over time, so the same money buys a little less each year. Around 3% a year is common.

needsWants.definition: Needs are must-pay bills like rent, power and groceries. Wants are nice-to-haves like eating out, shopping and subscriptions.

balanceTransfer.definition: Moving what you owe on one credit card to another card with lower (often 0%) interest for a while, usually for a one-off fee.

lakhCrore.definition: Ways of counting big amounts in Pakistan and India. 1 lakh = 100,000. 1 crore = 100 lakh = 10,000,000.

budgetData.p1: Everything you type into the calculator, including your take-home pay, bills, loans, subscriptions, yearly costs, goals and the ideas you add to your plan, is calculated by code running in your browser. None of it is uploaded to our servers or anyone else’s. We have no copy of it, so we can’t see it, sell it or lose it in a data breach.
budgetData.p2: The calculator also never asks for bank logins, account numbers or card numbers. Please don’t send them to us either.

device.title: What is stored on your device

table.budgetWhy: Remembers your numbers, plan choices, goals and settings between visits.
table.historyWhy: Keeps the months you save so you can compare them. Up to 60 months.
table.themeWhy: Remembers which colour theme you chose.

device.p1_html: So that your numbers are still there when you come back, the site saves them in your browser’s local storage. This is a small storage area that belongs to your browser on this device. It is not a cookie and it is not sent over the internet.
device.p2_html: To delete it: open the calculator, choose Edit my numbers → Start over, then Clear my numbers (keeps your saved months) or Delete everything. You can also clear this site’s data in your browser settings. Anyone who uses your device and browser can see what is stored, so use a private window on a shared computer.

sharing.title: Share links, backups, printing and reminders
sharing.p1: These features only run when you choose them, and none of them upload your budget to us:
sharing.item1_html: Share links. When you press Make a share link, your numbers are packed into the link itself, after the “#” sign. Browsers don’t send that part of a link to the website, so we never receive it. Anyone you give the link to can see the numbers in it, so share it only with people you trust.
sharing.item2_html: Backups. Download backup saves a file to your device. Opening a backup reads it in your browser.
sharing.item3_html: Printing and calendar reminders. The printable plan and the payday reminder file are made on your device.

contactData.title: When you contact us
contactData.p2: The form is delivered to our inbox by a third-party form service, which processes the message on our behalf and is not allowed to use it for anything else. We keep messages for up to 12 months after the conversation ends, then delete them, unless we need them longer to deal with a legal claim. We never add you to a mailing list and never sell or rent your details.
contactData.p3: Please don’t include personal financial details, such as account numbers or passwords, in a message. We don’t need them to help you.
contactData.p1_html: If you use our contact form or email us, we receive your name, your email address, the topic you choose, your message and the page you were on. We use this only to read and answer your message, fix problems you report and improve the site. Our legal basis is our legitimate interest in replying to you, or the steps you ask us to take.

ads.title: Advertising and cookies
ads.p1: The site is free because it shows ads. Ads are served by Google AdSense. We don’t give Google, or any advertiser, the numbers you enter in the calculator.
ads.item1: Third-party vendors, including Google, use cookies to serve ads based on your previous visits to this website and other websites.
ads.item2: Google’s use of advertising cookies lets it and its partners serve ads to you based on your visits to this site and other sites on the internet.
ads.p2: If you are in the European Economic Area, the UK or Switzerland, you’ll be asked for consent before personalised ads or their cookies are used, and you can change your choice at any time. If you decline, you may still see non-personalised ads, which rely on context rather than your browsing history. Ad-blocking or blocking third-party cookies in your browser also stops personalised ads, and the calculator keeps working either way.
ads.p3: The site itself sets no cookies, and we don’t use analytics or tracking tools.
ads.item3_html: You can opt out of personalised advertising in Google Ads Settings. You can also opt out of some third-party vendors’ personalised ads at aboutads.info or, in Europe, youronlinechoices.eu.
ads.item4_html: Learn more in how Google uses information from sites or apps that use its services.

logs.title: Hosting and security logs
logs.p1: Like every website, the site is delivered by a hosting provider. When your browser asks for a page, the host may briefly record technical details such as your IP address, browser type, the page requested and the time. These logs are used only to deliver the site, keep it secure and fix faults, and are deleted on the host’s normal schedule. They never contain your budget numbers.

rights.title: Your privacy rights
rights.p1: Because your budget never leaves your device, you already hold all of it, and you can delete it yourself at any time. For anything else we hold about you, such as messages you sent us, you can ask us to:
rights.item1: tell you what we hold and give you a copy;
rights.item4: stop or limit how we use it, or object to it.
rights.p2: These rights come from laws such as the EU and UK GDPR, the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA/CPRA) and India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, and similar laws elsewhere. We don’t sell or share personal information for money, and we don’t use it to make automated decisions about you.
rights.p3_html: To make a request, or to raise a grievance under India’s DPDP Act, use the contact form and choose Privacy or data request. We’ll reply within 30 days. You can withdraw any consent you gave, such as for personalised ads, at any time. You also have the right to complain to your local data protection authority, such as the ICO in the UK.

children.title: Children
children.p1: The site is meant for adults managing a household budget. It isn’t directed at children under 13 (under 16 in the EEA and UK, and under 18 in India), and we don’t knowingly collect personal information from them. If you think a child has sent us personal information, please contact us and we will delete it.

transfers.title: International transfers
transfers.p1: Messages you send us, and data used by Google for ads, may be processed in countries other than yours, including the United States. Where the law requires it, these transfers are protected by safeguards such as the European Commission’s standard contractual clauses.

links.title: Links to other websites
links.p1: Our money tips and ads may link to other websites. We don’t control them and aren’t responsible for their privacy practices, so please read their policies before giving them any information.

changes.title: Changes to this policy
changes.p1: We may update this policy when the site or the law changes. The date at the top shows the latest version. If a change affects how we handle information you have already given us, we’ll make it clear on the site before it takes effect.

contact.title: Contact
contact.p1_html: Questions about this policy or your data? Send us a message and choose Privacy or data request. You can also read our Terms of Use.

terms.lead: These terms explain what you can expect from the Household Budget Optimizer and what we ask of you. We’ve kept them short and in plain English.

summary.item1_html: It’s free for personal household budgeting. No account needed.
summary.item2_html: It’s an estimate, not advice. Check important decisions with a qualified professional.
summary.item3_html: Your numbers are yours. They stay in your browser, so keep a backup if they matter to you.
summary.item4_html: Please use it fairly. Don’t copy the site, attack it or scrape it.

agreement.title: 1. Agreeing to these terms
agreement.p1_html: By using the Household Budget Optimizer & Savings Simulator website and calculator (“the site”, “we”, “us”), you agree to these terms and to our Privacy Policy. If you don’t agree, please don’t use the site.

service.title: 2. What the tool is
service.p1: The site is a free budgeting calculator and money guide for personal, household use. It helps you see where your money goes, try ideas for spending less and estimate how savings, goals and debts could change over time. It runs in your web browser and doesn’t need an account.
service.p2: We may add, change or remove features, or pause the site for maintenance, at any time. Because it’s a free service, we can’t promise it will always be available or free of errors.

notAdvice.title: 3. Not financial advice
notAdvice.p2: Before making important money decisions, such as taking on or repaying debt, investing, or changing insurance, speak to a qualified, licensed financial adviser, accountant or tax professional. If you’re struggling with debt, free and confidential debt advice services are available in many countries.
notAdvice.p1_html: Everything on the site, including results, savings ideas, health scores, growth projections, debt-free dates and articles, is general information for education only. It is not financial, investment, tax, legal or debt advice, and it doesn’t take your full circumstances into account. Nothing on the site is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any financial product.

accuracy.title: 4. Estimates and accuracy
accuracy.p1: Results are only as good as the numbers you enter and the assumptions behind them. In particular:
accuracy.item1: savings percentages are typical estimates, and what you can actually save depends on your providers, location, prices and habits;
accuracy.item2: growth projections assume a steady return compounded monthly and ignore taxes and fees, while real investments go up and down and can lose value;
accuracy.item3: “typical” household amounts are rough guides, and for some currencies they are based on US figures;
accuracy.item4: the site doesn’t convert between currencies or use live interest or exchange rates.
accuracy.p2_html: We work hard to keep the maths correct, but we don’t guarantee that every result, figure or tip is complete, accurate or up to date. Please check anything important yourself. If you spot a mistake, tell us and we’ll look into it.

yourData.title: 5. Your data and backups
yourData.p1_html: Your budget is stored only in your browser on your device. We don’t have a copy, so we can’t recover it if it’s lost. Clearing your browser data, using a private window, or switching device or browser can remove it. Use Download backup to keep a copy. You are responsible for the share links and backup files you create and who you give them to.

use.title: 6. Fair use
use.p1: You may use the site for your own personal or household budgeting, and you may share links to it. You agree not to:
use.item1: copy, republish, sell or frame the site or its content as your own, or remove our notices;
use.item2: scrape the site in bulk, or overload, attack, probe or interfere with it or its security;
use.item3: upload or send anything harmful, such as malware, or use the site or contact form for spam, abuse or anything unlawful;
use.item4: use the site to give paid advice to others in a way that suggests we endorse it.
use.p2: We may block access for anyone who breaks these rules.

You may print or save your own results and the plan you make for personal use. Short quotes with a link back to the site are welcome. For anything else, please ask us first.

thirdParty.p1: The site shows ads, mostly served by Google, and may link to other websites. Ads and links are not endorsements. We don’t control other websites or the products advertised, and we aren’t responsible for their content, offers or privacy practices. Any deal you make with an advertiser is between you and them.

warranty.title: 9. No warranty
warranty.p1: The site is provided free, “as is” and “as available”. To the fullest extent the law allows, we make no promises or warranties of any kind, express or implied, including that the site will be accurate, reliable, uninterrupted, secure or fit for a particular purpose.

liability.title: 10. Limits of liability
liability.p1: To the fullest extent the law allows, we are not liable for any loss or damage arising from your use of, or inability to use, the site, or from relying on its results or content. This includes financial loss, lost savings or profits, lost data, and indirect or consequential loss. You use the results at your own risk and are responsible for your own financial decisions.
liability.p2: Nothing in these terms limits liability that can’t be limited by law, such as for fraud, or removes rights you have as a consumer under the laws of the country where you live.

law.p1: These terms are governed by the laws of the country where the site’s operator is based, and its courts will deal with any dispute. seeBudget.q: Can you see my budget numbers?
seeBudget.a: No. The calculator runs in your browser and never sends your numbers to us. That also means we can’t look at your budget to help, so please describe the problem in your message instead.

restore.q: My numbers disappeared. Can you restore them?
restore.a_html: We don’t have a copy, so we can’t. They’re saved in the browser you used, so check you’re on the same device and browser, outside a private window. Use Download backup on the History tab to keep a copy in future.

chillerFee.label: District cooling (chiller) bill
chillerFee.help: If your building’s air-conditioning comes from a district cooling company (for example Empower or Emicool), its monthly bill. This is separate from DEWA, ADDC or SEWA. Leave at 0 if cooling is included in your rent or comes from your own AC units.

housingFee.label: Municipality housing fee
housingFee.help: In Dubai, renters pay a housing fee of 5% of the yearly rent, added to the DEWA bill in monthly instalments. Other emirates charge similar fees (Abu Dhabi’s is collected with the ADDC bill). Enter what you pay each month.

privateHealth.label: Private health insurance
privateHealth.help: Your monthly hospital and/or extras cover premium after the government rebate. Optional, but many people hold hospital cover to avoid the Medicare levy surcharge.

condominio.label: Building fee (condomínio)
condominio.help: Your monthly condomínio fee for the building or gated community, if you pay it separately from rent.

planoSaude.label: Health plan (plano de saúde)
planoSaude.help: Your monthly health-plan bill, including any co-payments. If your employer pays it in full, leave this empty.

rundfunkbeitrag.label: Broadcast fee (Rundfunkbeitrag)
rundfunkbeitrag.help: The licence fee every household pays (€18.36 a month in 2026, usually billed every three months as €55.08).

comunidad.label: Community fees (comunidad)
comunidad.help: Monthly fee to your building’s owners’ association. Tenants usually have it included in the rent; leave it empty if so.

seguroMedico.label: Private health insurance
seguroMedico.help: Monthly premium for private health cover (e.g. Sanitas, Adeslas, DKV), if you have it.

mutuelle.label: Top-up health insurance (mutuelle)
mutuelle.help: Your monthly mutuelle (complémentaire santé). If your employer’s plan is taken from your payslip, leave this empty.

taxeFonciere.label: Property tax (taxe foncière)
taxeFonciere.help: Owners only: your yearly taxe foncière shown as a monthly amount. Tenants leave this empty.

councilTax.label: Council tax
councilTax.help: Your monthly council tax bill. Most councils bill in 10 instalments; spread it over 12 months here. Living alone usually gets 25% off.

tvLicence.label: TV licence
tvLicence.help: Needed to watch live TV or use BBC iPlayer. £180 a year from April 2026, about £15 a month.

galon.label: Drinking water (galon refills)
galon.help: Bottled drinking water — 19-litre galon refills from a depot or a brand like Aqua — as a monthly amount. Tap (PDAM) water goes in the water and gas box.

estateFees.label: Neighbourhood or building fees (IPL, iuran RT/RW)
estateFees.help: Monthly fees for your neighbourhood or building: iuran RT/RW, security, rubbish collection, or the apartment service charge (IPL) if it is not included in your rent.

arisan.label: Arisan contribution
arisan.help: Your monthly payment into an arisan — a rotating savings group where every member pays in and one member wins the whole pot each round. It works like saving rather than spending, so it is not an essential bill, but count it here so you know where the money goes.

societyMaintenance.label: Society maintenance
societyMaintenance.help: The monthly maintenance charge your housing society or apartment association collects (security, lifts, common areas, water pumps). Leave at 0 if it is already included in your rent.

powerBackup.label: Power backup (inverter or DG charges)
powerBackup.help: Diesel generator backup charged by your society, or inverter battery and UPS upkeep, as a monthly amount. Skip it if you have no backup.

chitFund.label: Chit fund / kitty payment
chitFund.help: Your monthly contribution to a chit fund, kitty or other rotating savings group. Each member pays in every month and takes the whole pot once. It works like saving, so it can be paused if money is tight, but count it here so you know where the money goes.

mantenimiento.label: Building maintenance fee (mantenimiento)
mantenimiento.help: Monthly maintenance fee for your building or gated community (cuota de mantenimiento), if it is not included in the rent.

gastosMedicos.label: Private medical insurance (gastos médicos mayores)
gastosMedicos.help: Your major-medical insurance premium shown as a monthly amount, if you pay for it yourself.

generatorFuel.label: Generator / inverter fuel
generatorFuel.help: Petrol or diesel for your generator (or for charging an inverter) when grid power is off, as a monthly amount. Don’t include the cost of buying the generator, inverter or batteries (add those as yearly costs).

estateDues.label: Estate dues and waste bill
estateDues.help: Monthly estate or landlord association dues (security, roads, street lights) and your waste collection bill (for example LAWMA in Lagos). If your service charge is paid yearly, enter it divided by 12.

esusu.label: Ajo / esusu contribution
esusu.help: Your monthly payment into an ajo, esusu or adashi — a rotating savings group where every member pays in and one member takes the whole pot each round. It works like saving rather than spending, so it is not an essential bill, but count it here so you know where the money goes.

generatorFuel.label: Generator / UPS running costs
generatorFuel.help: Petrol or diesel for a generator, plus UPS battery top-ups, during load-shedding — as a monthly amount. Don’t include the cost of buying the generator or UPS itself (add that as a yearly cost).

committee.label: Committee / BC payment
committee.help: Your monthly payment into a committee (BC) — a rotating savings group where every member pays in each month and one member takes the whole pot each turn. It works like saving rather than spending, so it is not an essential bill, but count it here so you know where the money goes.

dependentFee.label: Dependent fee (expats)
dependentFee.help: If you live in Saudi Arabia on an iqama, the government fee for each family member you sponsor (SAR 400 a month per person), usually paid for the whole year when the iqama is renewed. Enter it as a monthly amount. Leave at 0 if you are a Saudi citizen.

healthPremium.label: Health insurance premium
healthPremium.help: What you pay each month for health insurance, including the amount taken from your paycheck for an employer plan or a Marketplace plan after any tax credit.

ae-rent-cheques.label: Rent
ae-rent-cheques.title: Offer fewer rent cheques for a lower rent
ae-rent-cheques.why: Rent is agreed per year and paid in 1–12 post-dated cheques. Landlords often take less if you pay in 1 or 2 cheques. Enter your rent here as the yearly amount divided by 12.
ae-rent-cheques.evidence: Paying in fewer cheques often saves

tips.1: Ask what the rent would be with 1 or 2 cheques instead of 4 or more.
tips.2: Check the RERA rental index calculator before renewing: it shows whether your landlord can raise the rent.
tips.3: Start looking 90 days before your contract ends; landlords must give 90 days’ notice of any increase.

ae-dewa-slab.label: Electricity
ae-dewa-slab.title: Keep electricity out of the higher DEWA slabs
ae-dewa-slab.why: DEWA charges more per kWh as your monthly use moves through its slabs, so the summer AC months cost far more per unit.
ae-dewa-slab.evidence: Keeping use out of the top slabs usually cuts

tips.1: Set the AC to 24°C or higher and use timers so it isn’t cooling empty rooms.
tips.2: Get the AC ducts and filters cleaned before summer.
tips.3: Compare your monthly kWh on the DEWA app with the slab limits on your bill.

ae-salik-nol.label: Fares & tolls
ae-salik-nol.title: Cut Salik gates and use Nol for the commute
ae-salik-nol.why: Each Salik crossing costs AED 6.30 at peak and 4.20 off-peak; four peak crossings a working day add up to over AED 500 a month.
ae-salik-nol.evidence: Fewer peak Salik crossings and a Nol card for some trips usually cut

tips.1: Check if a route without Salik gates adds only a few minutes.
tips.2: Travel just before 6 am or after 8 pm when the toll is lower.
tips.3: Try the Metro with a Nol card a few days a week and compare the cost.

au-energy-made-easy.label: Electricity
au-energy-made-easy.title: Compare your electricity plan on Energy Made Easy
au-energy-made-easy.why: Many households are on plans priced at or near the Default Market Offer, while market offers from the same or other retailers are often cheaper.
au-energy-made-easy.evidence: Moving to a cheaper market offer often cuts

tips.1: Upload your bill to Energy Made Easy (or Victorian Energy Compare in Victoria) to see cheaper plans for your actual usage.
tips.2: Ask your current retailer to match the best offer before switching.
tips.3: If you have solar or can shift usage, compare time-of-use plans with cheap midday rates.

au-health-cover-review.label: Private health cover
au-health-cover-review.title: Review your private health cover tier and extras
au-health-cover-review.why: Premiums rise every April, and many people pay for extras or hospital services they never use.
au-health-cover-review.evidence: Dropping cover and extras you don’t use usually cuts

tips.1: Compare policies on privatehealth.gov.au, the government’s free comparison site.
tips.2: Check whether you use your extras enough to beat the premium; if not, drop extras or pick a cheaper tier.
tips.3: A higher excess lowers the premium; consider paying annually before 1 April to lock in the old price.

br-sair-do-rotativo.label: Credit cards
br-sair-do-rotativo.title: Get off the card rotativo now
br-sair-do-rotativo.why: The card rotativo averaged about 445% a year in August 2026 and the bill-instalment plan about 192% a year. Almost any other credit is cheaper.
br-sair-do-rotativo.evidence: Moving the balance to a much cheaper loan avoids

tips.1: Pay the full card bill if you possibly can; paying only the minimum puts the rest on the rotativo.
tips.2: If you can’t, swap the balance for a payroll-deducted loan (consignado) or a personal loan at a much lower rate instead of the bank’s instalment offer.
tips.3: Renegotiate overdue card debt through your bank or Serasa Limpa Nome, where discounts are common.

br-bandeira-chuveiro.label: Electricity
br-bandeira-chuveiro.title: Tame the electric shower and the bandeira
br-bandeira-chuveiro.why: Electric showers are one of the biggest power users in Brazilian homes, and red-flag (bandeira vermelha) months add a surcharge to every kWh.
br-bandeira-chuveiro.evidence: Shorter showers on the summer setting usually cut

tips.1: Set the shower to the "verão" (summer) setting and keep showers to 5–8 minutes.
tips.2: Check the bandeira on your bill and cut AC and dryer use in red-flag months.
tips.3: Ask your distributor whether you qualify for the Tarifa Social discount.

ca-phone-flanker.label: Internet & phone
ca-phone-flanker.title: Move your phone plan to a lower-cost brand
ca-phone-flanker.why: The big three carriers own cheaper brands on the same networks, and their plans often cost much less for the same data.
ca-phone-flanker.evidence: Moving to a lower-cost brand on the same network often cuts

tips.1: Compare your plan with Fizz, Public Mobile, Lucky Mobile, Koodo, Freedom or Virgin Plus; you can keep your number.
tips.2: Call your internet provider’s retention department and ask for the new-customer price, or switch.
tips.3: If you pay off a phone through your plan, check when it ends and move to a cheaper bring-your-own-phone plan.

ca-home-energy-rebates.label: Water & gas
ca-home-energy-rebates.title: Use home energy rebates before winter
ca-home-energy-rebates.why: Heating is the biggest energy cost in most Canadian homes, and provinces and utilities pay for many upgrades.
ca-home-energy-rebates.evidence: Rebate-funded insulation and heating upgrades usually cut

tips.1: Check your province’s and gas utility’s rebate programs (for example Enbridge or FortisBC) for insulation, smart thermostats and heat pumps.
tips.2: Seal drafts around doors and windows and turn the heat down 2–3°C at night and when you are out.
tips.3: If your utility offers equal monthly billing, use it to avoid winter bill shocks (it does not lower the total).

de-energy-switch.label: Electricity
de-energy-switch.title: Leave the default electricity tariff
de-energy-switch.why: Households still on the local supplier’s default tariff (Grundversorgung) pay around 40 ct/kWh, while the cheapest new-customer tariffs are around 30 ct/kWh.
de-energy-switch.evidence: Leaving the default tariff usually cuts

tips.1: Find your yearly kWh on your last bill and compare tariffs on Check24 or Verivox.
tips.2: Pick a tariff with a 12-month price guarantee and no prepayment.
tips.3: Set a reminder to compare again before the first year ends, when bonuses run out.

de-gas-switch.label: Water & gas
de-gas-switch.title: Switch your gas supplier
de-gas-switch.why: Gas prices for new customers are well below the default tariff and many long-standing contracts.

tips.1: Compare gas tariffs with your yearly kWh from the last statement.
tips.2: Check your monthly prepayment (Abschlag) matches your real use so you avoid a big back-payment.
tips.3: Bleed radiators and turn the heating down 1°C; each degree saves about 6%.

de-jobticket.label: Fares & tolls
de-jobticket.title: Ask for a Deutschlandticket Job
de-jobticket.why: If your employer pays at least 25% of the Deutschlandticket, the price drops a further 5%, so your share can fall well below €63.

tips.1: Ask HR whether they offer the Deutschlandticket Job.
tips.2: Cancel single tickets and local monthly passes the Deutschlandticket already covers.
tips.3: Check whether your state offers a cheaper student or social version.

es-pvpc-vs-libre.label: Electricity
es-pvpc-vs-libre.title: Check PVPC against a fixed-price tariff
es-pvpc-vs-libre.why: The regulated PVPC follows wholesale prices hour by hour; depending on your habits a fixed-price free-market tariff may be cheaper, or the other way round.
es-pvpc-vs-libre.evidence: Being on the tariff that suits your habits usually cuts

tips.1: Compare with the CNMC comparison tool using your last bills.
tips.2: Lower your contracted power (potencia) if you never trip the fuse.
tips.3: Run the washing machine and dishwasher in the off-peak hours (00:00–08:00 and weekends).

es-revolving.label: Credit cards
es-revolving.title: Get out of revolving credit
es-revolving.why: Revolving cards charge around 22–24% TAE, and low fixed payments can keep you in debt for years.
es-revolving.evidence: Paying off revolving credit with a cheaper loan avoids

tips.1: Switch the card from "pago aplazado" to paying the full balance each month.
tips.2: Ask your bank for a personal loan (~7% average) to clear the card.
tips.3: If your card charged far above the market average when you signed, ask a consumer association (OCU, Asufin) whether it may be usurious.

es-abono-transporte.label: Fares & tolls
es-abono-transporte.title: Use the subsidised monthly pass
es-abono-transporte.why: Regional and state-subsidised passes (abono joven, abono único) are much cheaper than single tickets for regular commuters.
es-abono-transporte.evidence: A subsidised monthly pass usually cuts

tips.1: Check your region’s monthly pass and the youth discount if you are under 26.
tips.2: Compare it with what you spend on single tickets and parking.
tips.3: Ask your employer about tax-free transport cards (tarjeta transporte).

fr-prime-transport.label: Fares & tolls
fr-prime-transport.title: Claim your 50% transit refund
fr-prime-transport.why: Employers must reimburse half of your public-transport pass (prime transport). Some people never claim it.
fr-prime-transport.evidence: Claiming the employer refund usually cuts

tips.1: Send your Navigo or local pass receipt to HR or payroll.
tips.2: Choose the yearly pass (Navigo Annuel) if you use it every month.
tips.3: Ask about the forfait mobilités durables if you cycle or carpool.

fr-energy-offer.label: Electricity
fr-energy-offer.title: Compare offers to the regulated tariff
fr-energy-offer.why: Many market offers are cheaper than the tarif réglementé (TRV), and the off-peak option can lower bills if you run appliances at night.
fr-energy-offer.evidence: A cheaper market offer usually cuts

tips.1: Compare offers on energie-info.fr, the national energy ombudsman’s comparison site.
tips.2: Check that your meter power (kVA) is not higher than you need.
tips.3: Ask whether you are eligible for the chèque énergie.

fr-loi-hamon.label: Car insurance
fr-loi-hamon.title: Switch insurer at any time after one year
fr-loi-hamon.why: Under the loi Hamon you can cancel home and car insurance at any time after the first year, and the new insurer handles it.
fr-loi-hamon.evidence: Switching insurer after the first year often cuts

tips.1: Get 3 quotes for the same cover and excess.
tips.2: Let the new insurer cancel the old contract for you.
tips.3: Combine home and car with one insurer for a discount.

gb-energy-switch.label: Electricity
gb-energy-switch.title: Check for a fixed energy deal below the price cap
gb-energy-switch.why: Most homes on a standard variable tariff pay the Ofgem price cap rate. Fixed deals and smart time-of-use tariffs are sometimes cheaper.
gb-energy-switch.evidence: A fixed deal below the price cap usually cuts

tips.1: Compare fixed tariffs against the current price cap on a comparison site before the next cap change (January, April, July, October).
tips.2: Give a meter reading and switch to paying by Direct Debit, which is cheaper than paying on receipt of bill.
tips.3: If you have a smart meter and can shift usage, look at time-of-use tariffs with cheaper overnight rates.

gb-council-tax-discount.label: Council tax
gb-council-tax-discount.title: Claim council tax discounts you are entitled to
gb-council-tax-discount.why: If only one adult lives in a home, the bill is 25% lower, and some bands are wrong.

tips.1: If you live alone (or the only other adults are students or apprentices), apply for the 25% single person discount on your council’s website.
tips.2: Check your band against similar homes on your street on the Valuation Office Agency (or Scottish Assessors) site.
tips.3: Ask your council about Council Tax Reduction if your income is low.

id-va-power.label: Electricity
id-va-power.title: Check your PLN power level and token habits
id-va-power.why: All households from 1,300 VA up pay the same Rp1,444.70 per kWh, so savings come from using fewer kWh, mainly AC and water heaters.
id-va-power.evidence: Running the AC and water heater less usually cuts

tips.1: Set the AC to 25–26°C with a timer and close doors to the room you are cooling.
tips.2: Buy prepaid tokens in larger amounts: the admin fee is per purchase.
tips.3: Swap old fluorescent tubes and incandescent bulbs for LED.

id-krl-tj.label: Fares & tolls
id-krl-tj.title: Mix KRL, TransJakarta and MRT instead of daily ojek
id-krl-tj.why: TransJakarta costs Rp3,500 a trip and KRL fares start from a few thousand rupiah, far below ride-hailing for the same distance.
id-krl-tj.evidence: Taking KRL, TransJakarta or MRT for regular trips usually cuts

tips.1: Use ojek only for the first and last kilometre to the station.
tips.2: Use one card (e.g. JakLingko-linked) so transfers are integrated and cheaper.
tips.3: Compare a week of ride-hailing receipts with the public transport cost of the same trips.

id-galon-depot.label: Drinking water
id-galon-depot.title: Switch branded galons for a trusted refill depot
id-galon-depot.why: Refilling at a licensed depot costs a fraction of branded galons.
id-galon-depot.evidence: A licensed refill depot usually cuts

tips.1: Choose a depot that shows a current health/hygiene certificate.
tips.2: Or boil and filter PDAM water for cooking.
tips.3: Buy galons in a monthly delivery plan if your depot offers one.

in-rooftop-solar.label: Electricity
in-rooftop-solar.title: Check the rooftop solar subsidy
in-rooftop-solar.why: If you own your home and the AC runs most of the year, a small rooftop system can wipe out most of a bill that sits in the higher slabs.
in-rooftop-solar.evidence: A small rooftop system usually cuts

tips.1: Look up PM Surya Ghar on the official portal: it pays a central subsidy for home rooftop solar up to 3 kW.
tips.2: Ask your DISCOM for a net meter so units you export are taken off your bill.
tips.3: Get 2–3 quotes from vendors on the DISCOM’s approved list before you pay anything.

in-lpg-subsidy.label: Water & gas
in-lpg-subsidy.title: Book LPG refills only when needed and claim any subsidy
in-lpg-subsidy.why: Cooking gas is most of the “water and gas” line in Indian homes.
in-lpg-subsidy.evidence: Careful LPG use and any subsidy usually cut

tips.1: Link your LPG connection to Aadhaar and your bank so any subsidy reaches your account.
tips.2: Use a pressure cooker and lids on pans: they cut cooking gas noticeably.
tips.3: If your building has piped gas (PNG), compare its cost per month with cylinder refills.

in-metro-card.label: Fares & tolls
in-metro-card.title: Use a metro smart card or monthly pass
in-metro-card.why: Metro smart cards and monthly bus passes are cheaper per trip than paying cash or taking autos and cabs every day.
in-metro-card.evidence: A metro card or monthly pass usually cuts

tips.1: Use a metro smart card or NCMC card instead of single tokens; many metros give a discount per trip.
tips.2: Check if your city bus service sells a monthly pass.
tips.3: Share cabs with colleagues for the last mile instead of solo rides.

mx-meses-sin-intereses.label: Shopping & extras
mx-meses-sin-intereses.title: Watch your "meses sin intereses"
mx-meses-sin-intereses.why: Interest-free instalments feel free, but several at once tie up future quincenas and push people into paying only the card minimum, where interest is around 55% a year.
mx-meses-sin-intereses.evidence: Taking on fewer new instalment plans usually cuts

tips.1: Add up every MSI instalment still running before buying anything new on instalments.
tips.2: Keep MSI payments to a small share of each quincena and never pay just the minimum.
tips.3: Ask for the cash price; some shops give a discount that MSI hides.

mx-tarifa-dac.label: Electricity
mx-tarifa-dac.title: Stay out of the DAC tariff
mx-tarifa-dac.why: CFE moves high-use homes to the unsubsidised DAC tariff based on 12 months of use, and getting out takes a year of lower use. Each block above basic use also costs more per kWh.
mx-tarifa-dac.evidence: Staying below the DAC limit usually cuts

tips.1: Check the "Tarifa" line and kWh blocks on your CFE bill.
tips.2: Run the AC at 25–26°C, and replace fridges and AC units over 10 years old with efficient models.
tips.3: Move ironing, washing and pumps out of the hottest hours.

mx-gas-lp.label: Water & gas
mx-gas-lp.title: Make each gas cylinder last longer
mx-gas-lp.why: Gas LP prices are capped weekly, but a family can go through one or two cylinders a month.
mx-gas-lp.evidence: Making each cylinder last longer usually cuts

tips.1: Check the weekly maximum price per kg for your area before you pay the delivery.
tips.2: Look for leaks with soapy water on the hose and regulator.
tips.3: Use lids on pots and a solar or efficient water heater if you can.

ng-solar-inverter.label: Generator fuel
ng-solar-inverter.title: Move from generator to a solar inverter
ng-solar-inverter.why: Generator fuel is often the single biggest power cost in Nigerian homes, and petrol and diesel prices swing with the exchange rate.

tips.1: Price a 2–5 kVA inverter with lithium batteries and a few solar panels; many vendors offer instalment plans.
tips.2: Run only fans, lights, TV and router on backup; save heavy loads for grid hours.
tips.3: Service the generator regularly and switch it off once the inverter is charged.

ng-meter-band.label: Electricity
ng-meter-band.title: Get a prepaid meter and check your band
ng-meter-band.why: Estimated (“crazy”) billing and paying Band A rates without Band A hours both inflate the electricity bill.
ng-meter-band.evidence: A prepaid meter on the right band usually cuts

tips.1: Apply for a prepaid meter through your DisCo’s MAP scheme instead of paying estimated bills.
tips.2: Track your supply hours for a week; if you get fewer than 20 a day on Band A, complain to the DisCo and NERC.
tips.3: Buy units through your bank app to avoid vendor charges.

ng-rent-yearly.label: Rent
ng-rent-yearly.title: Plan for rent paid a year or two in advance
ng-rent-yearly.why: Landlords usually ask for 1–2 years’ rent upfront, plus agency and legal fees. Enter rent here as the yearly amount divided by 12, and save towards the next payment every month.
ng-rent-yearly.evidence: Negotiating before you renew usually cuts

tips.1: Set aside the monthly share of next year’s rent in a separate savings account or money-market fund.
tips.2: Negotiate the renewal early, before the landlord advertises the flat.
tips.3: Ask if the landlord accepts rent in two halves instead of one lump sum.

pk-protected-slab.label: Electricity
pk-protected-slab.title: Stay in the protected 200-unit slab in winter
pk-protected-slab.why: Homes that use up to 200 units a month for six months in a row pay a much lower “protected” rate. One month over can cost you that status for the next six months.
pk-protected-slab.evidence: Staying in the protected slab usually cuts

tips.1: Check the last 6 months of “units” on your bill to see if you are close to protected status.
tips.2: In winter, switch off the geyser’s electric element and use gas or an instant geyser instead.
tips.3: Read your meter mid-month so you can cut back before you cross 200 units.

pk-solar-ups.label: Generator & UPS
pk-solar-ups.title: Swap generator hours for a solar + battery setup
pk-solar-ups.why: Petrol for a generator is one of the most expensive ways to make electricity. A small solar panel and lithium battery can cover fans, lights and the router during load-shedding.
pk-solar-ups.evidence: A solar and battery setup usually cuts

tips.1: Price a 1–3 kW solar kit with an inverter that can also charge from the grid.
tips.2: Run only fans, lights and Wi-Fi on backup; keep the AC and iron for grid hours.
tips.3: Service the generator and UPS batteries before summer so they don’t waste fuel or charge.

pk-gas-geyser.label: Water & gas
pk-gas-geyser.title: Fit a geyser timer or instant geyser
pk-gas-geyser.why: Gas geysers left on all day are a big part of winter gas bills, and gas tariffs rise steeply in higher slabs.
pk-gas-geyser.evidence: A geyser timer or instant geyser usually cuts

tips.1: Put a timer on the geyser so it heats water only morning and evening.
tips.2: Consider an instant (tankless) geyser when the old one needs replacing.
tips.3: Insulate the hot-water pipes on the roof.

sa-rent-instalments.label: Rent
sa-rent-instalments.title: Negotiate rent when you choose how often to pay
sa-rent-instalments.why: Rent is usually agreed per year on Ejar and paid in 1, 2 or 4 instalments. Enter it here as the yearly amount divided by 12. Paying in fewer instalments can earn a discount.
sa-rent-instalments.evidence: Paying in fewer instalments often saves

tips.1: Ask the landlord what the yearly rent would be if you paid in 1 or 2 instalments.
tips.2: Make sure the contract is registered on Ejar so increases follow the agreed terms.
tips.3: Compare similar flats in your district on listing apps 2 months before renewal.

sa-6000-kwh.label: Electricity
sa-6000-kwh.title: Stay under 6,000 kWh in summer months
sa-6000-kwh.why: Homes pay 18 halalas a kWh up to 6,000 kWh a month and 30 halalas above it, so the hottest months cost much more per unit for big villas.
sa-6000-kwh.evidence: Keeping summer use under 6,000 kWh usually cuts

tips.1: Check monthly kWh in the SEC app; aim to keep peak months under 6,000.
tips.2: Set split units to 24°C and switch off AC in empty rooms and majlis.
tips.3: Shade west-facing windows and service AC units before summer.

sa-bnpl.label: Shopping & extras
sa-bnpl.title: Limit buy-now-pay-later on everyday shopping
sa-bnpl.why: Splitting purchases into instalments makes it easy to spend more than planned each month.
sa-bnpl.evidence: Keeping instalment plans to essentials usually cuts

tips.1: Turn off instalment options as the default payment in shopping apps.
tips.2: Keep a running total of open instalment plans and their due dates.
tips.3: Wait 24 hours before buying anything over SAR 500.

us-open-enrollment.label: Health insurance
us-open-enrollment.title: Compare health plans at open enrollment
us-open-enrollment.why: Employer and Marketplace plans change prices every year, and the default is often to roll over into the same plan.
us-open-enrollment.evidence: Picking the right plan at open enrollment often cuts

tips.1: At open enrollment, compare the premium plus the deductible you realistically expect to pay, not the premium alone.
tips.2: If you are both covered at work, check whether one family plan or two separate plans costs less.
tips.3: If you buy on HealthCare.gov or a state Marketplace, update your income: you may qualify for a bigger tax credit.

about.title: About Budget Optimizer
about.lead: A free, private household budget calculator that helps families see where their money goes and find simple ways to keep more of it.

why.title: Why this tool exists
why.p1: Most households don’t lose money in one big way. It slips out through small, regular costs that are easy to miss: a subscription nobody uses, a bill that crept up, interest on a card. This tool helps you find those leaks and plug them.
why.p2: It is free, needs no sign-up and works in many countries and languages, because careful money planning shouldn’t depend on where you live or what you can pay for an app.

who.title: Who runs it
who.p1: Budget Optimizer is an independent project, built and looked after by a small team who want household money to be simpler to understand.

how.title: How the calculator works
how.item1_html: You enter your bills. Income, housing, utilities, transport, food, loans and subscriptions, as you pay them in a normal month. Costs that come once a year are spread over twelve months.
how.item2_html: We compare them with typical households. Each bill is set against a typical range for households like yours in the country you choose.
how.item3_html: We suggest changes, with the sum behind each. Every idea shows the bill it works on, the share it usually saves and the result, under “How did we get this?”. If two ideas cut the same bill, the second only counts what is left.
how.item4_html: Only what you choose counts. Ideas you add to your plan change your results. Interest you would avoid on debt is shown separately and is not counted as money saved each month.

numbers.title: Where the numbers come from
numbers.p1: Each country has its own file of typical amounts: income, rent, groceries, power, fuel, school fees and more, for three kinds of household. These are estimates for planning, not exact figures for your city, and some are still being checked against local data. For any other country, typical amounts are worked out as shares of your own income.
numbers.p2: The table shows when each country’s figures were last reviewed and how many sources were used. You can open the list of sources below it.

privacy.title: Your privacy
privacy.p1_html: Your budget is worked out in your own browser and is never sent to us. There is no account and nothing to sign up for. Ads keep the tool free. Read the full Privacy Policy.

standards.title: Editorial standards
standards.p1: Everything here is for general education. It is not financial, tax or legal advice, and it does not recommend any product or provider. Figures are estimates, and we say so when a number is uncertain.
standards.p2_html: Found a mistake, a figure that looks wrong or a broken link? Please tell us. We read every message and correct errors as soon as we can.
